hints: Do not get distracted by the huge size of $700 \mu m$ or the rod shape. Focus on where the DNA is and what shape it is.
Recall the defining difference in DNA organisation: free small circular DNA in the cytoplasm points to one cell type, while linear DNA inside a membrane-bound nucleus points to the other.
walkthrough:
**Sort the clues into helpful and distracting**

This organism is single-celled, rod-shaped, has a cell wall, and is $700 \mu m$ long. Size and shape alone cannot decide the answer, as a few giant bacteria are exceptionally large.

The most diagnostic clue is: thousands of copies of small, circular DNA in the cytoplasm.

**Apply the prokaryote versus eukaryote rule**

Prokaryotes have no true nucleus. Their genetic material is small, circular DNA lying free in the cytoplasm, often as plasmids as well as the main chromosome.

Eukaryotes have large, linear DNA enclosed in a membrane-bound nucleus, plus small circular DNA only inside mitochondria and chloroplasts, not free in thousands of copies.

**Conclude with confidence**

Free small circular DNA in the cytoplasm matches a prokaryote, most likely a giant bacterium. Cell wall and large size do not change this, so option D is correct.

options.A: Visibility without a microscope does not make a cell a eukaryote. Some giant prokaryotes can be seen with the naked eye.
options.B: It is very large for a prokaryote, but size is not the defining feature. A few giant bacteria reach hundreds of micrometres, so DNA structure is decisive.
options.C: Cell walls are not unique to plants. Prokaryotes, fungi and many protists also have cell walls, and a single cell living in a fish cannot be a plant.
options.D: Small, circular DNA free in the cytoplasm with no nucleus is the classic prokaryotic arrangement, so this is a prokaryote.
